*Prepared for CitiSense (HORIZON-CL2-2025-01-DEMOCRACY-03, GA 101286806), WP5 — Economic
Dimensions of Enlargement, Tasks 5.2 and 5.3. This document is the Polish counterpart to
Krisztina Szabó's* Hungarian Public Opinion Survey Datasets Overview *(12 August 2026) and
follows its structure so that the two national inventories can be read side by side.*

CBOS data archive (PADS/RDS): https://rds.icm.edu.pl/dataverse/CBOS \
ESS Data Portal: https://ess.sikt.no/ \
PGSW / Polish National Election Study: https://pgsw.edu.pl/


# 1. Introduction

This document provides an overview of the public opinion survey datasets covering Poland that
are suitable for examining the relationship between post-enlargement socioeconomic
disparities and support for populist, illiberal and eurosceptic political forces. It is the
Polish counterpart to the Hungarian dataset overview prepared for the same work package, and
is organised so that the two can be compared directly.

Two datasets carry the main analytical weight:

1. **CBOS "Aktualne problemy i wydarzenia" (APiW)** (1990–present): a Polish recurring
   cross-sectional omnibus survey conducted monthly by the CBOS Foundation (Fundacja Centrum
   Badania Opinii Społecznej). This is the functional equivalent of the Hungarian TÁRKI
   Omnibusz, but with a longer, denser and more completely archived time series.
2. **European Social Survey (ESS)** (2002–2024): the pan-European biennial survey coordinated
   by ESS ERIC. Poland has participated in every round to date, and is in the field for
   Round 12.

Three further sources are documented in Section 6 because they answer questions the two main
datasets cannot: the **Polish National Election Study (PGSW)**, the **Polish Panel Survey
(POLPAN)** and **Diagnoza Społeczna**.

The two main datasets are complementary in the same way as their Hungarian counterparts. CBOS
APiW provides high-frequency, Poland-specific measurement with a very long EU attitude series;
the ESS provides standardised cross-national comparability and documented methodological
control. There is, however, one important asymmetry relative to the Hungarian case, and it
works in Poland's favour: **both** Polish datasets carry a regional identifier at NUTS 2
level, whereas in Hungary the TÁRKI Omnibusz offers only settlement type. This is set out in
Section 7.

The appendices inventory the relevant questions. Appendix A catalogues 798 CBOS APiW
questions on European integration, globalisation, migration and international organisations,
drawn from 133 survey waves between 1992 and 2017. Appendix B catalogues the
corresponding ESS questions (2002–2023), with verbatim Polish wording.

## 1.1. Research Context

The 2004 enlargement of the European Union, of which Poland was much the largest new member,
transformed the socioeconomic structure of Central and Eastern Europe. Poland's trajectory
since accession differs from Hungary's in ways that matter for WP5's comparative design:

- Poland has been the largest net recipient of EU cohesion and agricultural funds in
  absolute terms since 2004, and the distribution of those funds across voivodeships and
  subregions is highly uneven. This makes Poland the central case for Task 5.2's analysis of
  subnational variation in EU fund governance.
- Aggregate support for EU membership has remained extremely high throughout — CBOS has
  recorded it continuously since 1994 — while political conflict over the EU intensified
  sharply between 2015 and 2023. Poland therefore offers the analytically useful combination
  of *stable majority support* with *rising elite and partisan polarisation*, which is
  precisely the configuration in which aggregate figures conceal the socioeconomic and
  regional divides Task 5.3 is designed to detect.
- The 2015–2016 refugee crisis produced a large and abrupt shift in attitudes to migration
  that is densely measured in the CBOS series. Because it can be observed at monthly
  resolution, the Polish data can identify the timing of attitude change far more precisely
  than biennial cross-national surveys allow.

Both datasets are suited to this agenda because they cover the pre- and post-accession
periods with long time series, measure attitudes to the EU and to democratic institutions
repeatedly, contain the key political preference and socioeconomic variables, and rest on
representative national probability samples.

# 3. Dataset 1: CBOS "Aktualne problemy i wydarzenia"

## 3.1. What is the APiW survey?

"Aktualne problemy i wydarzenia" (Current Problems and Events) is the statutory monthly
survey of the CBOS Foundation, conducted since 1990. Like the Hungarian Omnibusz, it consists
of a stable core administered in every wave together with rotating blocks that change from
month to month. CBOS publishes 160–200 research reports (*komunikaty z badań*) per year drawn
from this series; the reports are the public face of the data, but the microdata and the full
questionnaires are separately archived (Section 3.6).

CBOS is a public foundation established by statute, which distinguishes it from a commercial
polling house: the statutory survey programme is not client-driven, its results are published
in full, and the questionnaires are deposited. For the purposes of WP5 this matters because
the EU-related items were asked as part of a continuing public-interest programme rather than
commissioned episodically, which is why the series is as long and as regular as it is.

## 3.2. Methodology

**Sampling.** Stratified, multi-stage random sample of adults (18+) drawn as a *named*
(imienna) sample from the PESEL population register. The population of each of the 16
voivodeships is stratified by six settlement-size classes — village; town up to 19,999;
20,000–49,999; 50,000–99,999; 100,000–499,999; and cities above 500,000 (Warsaw, Kraków,
Łódź, Poznań, Wrocław). Rural populations in Mazowieckie (left/right bank of the Vistula) and
Śląskie (Silesia proper vs. the Dąbrowa Basin) are split further. Because most voivodeships
contain fewer than six settlement classes, and small strata are merged, the realised design
has used approximately 79–80 strata in recent years rather than the notional 96.

**Selection.** Two- or three-stage depending on stratum type. In urban strata, localities are
drawn with probability proportional to size without replacement, then one cluster of
respondents is drawn within each selected locality. In rural strata, a gmina/rural area is
drawn PPS, then a village within it PPS, then a cluster. Strata consisting of a single
locality (e.g. a large voivodeship capital) are single-stage. Clusters have comprised 9
respondents; a recent annual sample design drew 330 clusters, i.e. 2,971 named individuals
per wave, to achieve roughly 1,000 interviews.

**Sample size.** Typically c. 1,000 respondents per wave (e.g. 1,020 achieved from 2,971
drawn in March 2017; 938 in January 2026).

**Data collection.** Face-to-face interviews (CAPI) until 2020. Since May 2020 CBOS has run
the statutory surveys as a **mixed-mode** design in which each named respondent chooses
between CAPI, CATI (telephone, using contact details supplied in an advance letter) and CAWI
(self-completion online, using a login supplied in the advance letter). The instrument is
identical across modes, and CBOS reports the mode split for every wave (January 2026: 55.5%
CAPI, 26.4% CATI, 18.0% CAWI).

**Fieldwork control.** Minimum three contact attempts, required at different times of day and
on different days of the week; substitution of respondents is not permitted; 5–10% of
completed interviews are back-checked in line with OFBOR standards.

**Weighting.** Post-stratification by rim (iterative proportional fitting) weighting to GUS
and PESEL demographic benchmarks on sex, urban/rural settlement class, voivodeship of
residence, age group, education and socio-occupational group.

**Frequency.** Monthly, approximately 12 waves per year.

**Language.** Questionnaires are in Polish. There is no routine English translation, although
CBOS publishes an English-language summary series (*Polish Public Opinion*).

## 3.3. Survey structure

Each wave has two parts:

1. **Core module** — administered every wave: sociodemographics drawn partly from the sample
   frame (sex, year of birth, settlement size class, voivodeship), party preference and
   turnout intention, evaluation of the government and of named politicians, trust in
   institutions, and the standard "social mood" battery on the country's economic and
   political situation and on household material conditions.
2. **Rotating blocks** — a variable set of questions that changes monthly, covering topical
   subjects. EU-related content appears here, which is why its coverage is uneven across
   waves and is concentrated around politically salient moments.

## 3.4. Temporal coverage

- **1990–1997**: Pre-accession; attitudes to the European Communities/EU as a distant
  prospect, and to NATO membership.
- **1998–2002**: Accession negotiations; dense measurement of expected costs and benefits,
  and of referendum vote intention.
- **June 2003**: EU accession referendum (77.45% in favour on 58.85% turnout).
- **1 May 2004**: Accession.
- **2004–2014**: Post-accession evaluation, labour mobility, euro adoption, the
  Constitutional and Lisbon treaties, EU funds.
- **2015–2017**: Refugee crisis and the change of government; the densest concentration of
  migration items in the whole series.
- **2018–present**: Rule-of-law conflict, "Polexit" debate, Brexit, and — after February 2022
  — Ukrainian refugees and enlargement to Ukraine. This period is covered by the published
  *komunikaty* but not by the open microdata archive.

## 3.6. Access and archiving

CBOS has deposited the APiW microdata with the **Polish Social Data Archive** (Polskie
Archiwum Danych Społecznych, PADS), published through the **Social Data Repository**
(Repozytorium Danych Społecznych, RDS) at `rds.icm.edu.pl`. There are 329 deposited waves.
Access is free after registration, and all but one of the deposits carry a CC BY-SA 4.0
licence.

Each deposit contains three files: the data in SPSS (`.sav`) and Stata formats, and a
documentation PDF (`_DOK.pdf`) that runs to roughly 200–250 pages. The documentation is the
reason this archive is unusually valuable for the present purpose. It contains, for every
wave: the topic list with keywords; the full sampling and weighting documentation; and **the
complete verbatim questionnaire**, including question numbers, exact Polish wording, response
categories and the corresponding variable names. Appendix A is built directly from these
documents.

Two practical notes:

- **Two documentation formats.** Waves up to roughly 2008 use a typeset PAPI questionnaire
  with plain numeric question identifiers (`21.`, `22.`). Later waves are exports from the
  CADAS CAPI scripting system, with letter-prefixed identifiers (`E1.`, `M12A.`,
  `P7.`), inline variable names (`q86 (single)`) and placeholder tokens (`%tpu%` for
  "trudno powiedzieć", `%oo%` for refusal). Both are readable, but text extracted
  programmatically needs format-aware parsing, and question numbering is not comparable
  across the break.
- **The archive stops at December 2017.** The deposits were published in 2021, but the
  fieldwork they cover runs from January 1990 to December 2017 (APiW waves 1–331). Coverage
  within that window is complete: twelve waves per year from 1993 onward, eleven in 1990 and
  1991, eight in 1992. The monthly series itself continues without interruption, and the
  *komunikaty* for recent years report the EU items with their measurement dates — the
  membership-support series is published as a continuous trend from 1994 to the present.
  Microdata for waves after 2017 must be requested from CBOS directly. For WP5, any analysis
  needing individual-level data past 2017 will require that request; the published aggregate
  series is sufficient for establishing trend context.


# 4. Dataset 2: European Social Survey (Poland)

## 4.1. What is the ESS?

The European Social Survey is an academically driven cross-national survey conducted across
Europe every two years since 2002. It was awarded European Research Infrastructure Consortium
(ERIC) status in 2013. **Poland has participated in all eleven released rounds and is in the
field for Round 12**, giving an unbroken biennial series from 2002. The Polish national
coordination has been based at the Institute of Philosophy and Sociology of the Polish
Academy of Sciences (IFiS PAN).

## 4.2. Methodology

**Sampling.** Stratified random probability sampling of persons aged 15+ resident in private
households. The Polish sample is drawn from the PESEL register as a named individual sample.

**Sample size.** Typically c. 1,500–2,000 achieved interviews per round in Poland.

**Data collection.** Face-to-face interviews (CAPI). Round 10 was fielded by self-completion
in Poland because of COVID-19, which changed the questionnaire layout and question numbering
(Section 4.5).

**Response rates.** Documented per round; Round 9 (fieldwork 26 October 2018 – 20 March 2019)
achieved 43.31%.

**Frequency.** Biennial.

**Languages.** Fielded in Polish; source questionnaire in English. Polish is a "shared
language" in ESS terms, also fielded in Iceland in recent rounds.

**Standards.** ESS Sampling Guidelines, Translation Guidelines (TRAPD) and Questionnaire
Design Protocols apply, with published quality and documentation reports per round.

## 4.3. Survey structure

Each round comprises a **core module** repeated every round (media use, social and
institutional trust, politics, subjective well-being, national/ethnic/religious allegiance,
social values, demographics, socioeconomic background) and **two rotating modules** selected
by open academic competition.

For WP5 the rounds that carry most weight are **ESS7 (2014)**, for its detailed immigration
module immediately before the refugee crisis; **ESS8 (2016)**, which introduced the EU
membership referendum item and a block on EU-level redistribution and EU-level
decision-making; and **ESS11 (2023)**, the first round fielded after the 2023 Polish election.

## 4.5. Poland-specific features and deviations

Three features of the Polish ESS series need to be known before the data are used, and none
of them is obvious from the codebook alone.

1. **`euftf` is missing in Round 5.** The item on European unification having "gone too far"
   or needing to "go further" was not fielded in 2010. This is not a Polish deviation: the
   ESS5 source questionnaire states that "Question B34 has been excluded for Round 5.
   Showcard 13 will not be used in Round 5", and the Polish questionnaire records the
   deletion in the corresponding place ("PYTANIE B34 I KARTA 13 ZOSTAŁY USUNIĘTE"). Any
   longitudinal series on this item has a structural gap at 2010 for every country.
2. **Round 10 uses a different numbering scheme.** Because Poland fielded R10 by
   self-completion, questions carry a single A-series numbering (`A22`, `A50`, `A90`)
   rather than the usual B/C/E blocks. The R10 documentation includes an explicit mapping
   table from source question number to self-completion question number to variable name;
   the variables themselves are unchanged.
3. **The regional identifier is not designed for regional inference.** The ESS9
   documentation for Poland records "Statistical inference possible at the regional level:
   No", and recommends grouping the 16 NUTS 2 categories into six NUTS 1 groups by first
   digit for analysis. This is a real constraint on Task 5.2: the ESS can characterise broad
   macroregional contrasts in Poland, but it is not a vehicle for voivodeship-level
   estimates. Where voivodeship-level precision is needed, pooled CBOS waves are the better
   instrument.


# 5. Dataset 3: Polish National Election Study (PGSW)

The *Polskie Generalne Studium Wyborcze* (PGSW) is Poland's national election study, fielded
after each parliamentary election since 1997 (1997, 2001, 2005, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019,
2023). It carries the CSES module, which makes it comparable with some 50 electoral
democracies, and it is the standard source for Polish voting behaviour.

Three things recommend it for WP5. First, it measures vote choice directly and validly, which
neither CBOS nor the ESS does with the same precision — and Task 5.3 is about the link between
socioeconomic experience and *political behaviour*, not attitudes alone. Second, it contains
EU-specific items: the 2019 study includes a foreign-policy placement scale running from
"closest possible cooperation with the European Union, and observance of its binding rules"
to "defence of our political and economic independence, even at the cost of leaving the
European Union", and a direct item on whether EU membership will bring Poland more benefits
than dangers over the next decade. Third, **PGSW 2023 is based at SWPS University**, the WP5
lead, which removes access friction for the most recent and most politically consequential
edition.

PGSW 2023 fielded a CAPI sample of 1,500 and a CAWI sample of 2,000 within one to three weeks
of the election. Earlier editions are deposited in PADS/RDS and, for some years, in Harvard
Dataverse; access conditions are more restrictive than for CBOS and require registration and
approval.

# 6. Further Polish data sources

**POLPAN (Polski Sondaż Panelowy)**, at IFiS PAN, is one of the longest-running panel studies
in Europe: initiated in 1987–88 with 5,817 respondents aged 21–65, reduced to a target panel
of 2,500 in 1993, and fielded at five-year intervals since, with youngest-cohort refreshment
samples from 1998. It is the only Polish source that can identify *within-person* change in
socioeconomic position across the accession period, which is what distinguishes a genuine
test of the "losers of transition" hypothesis from a cross-sectional association. Its
weakness for present purposes is a thin EU attitude battery.

**Diagnoza Społeczna** (2000–2015) combined household and individual panel measurement with
unusually detailed material-conditions data. It is discontinued, but for the 2004–2015 window
it remains the richest Polish source on objective household economic circumstances measured
alongside attitudes.

**PGSS (Polski Generalny Sondaż Społeczny)** carried the ISSP modules for Poland and provides
the closest Polish analogue to the ISSP content that appears in the Hungarian Omnibusz
rotating modules.

**Eurobarometer** provides harmonised EU attitude measurement for Poland from 2001 (candidate
country barometers) and continuously since accession. Its sampling and mode documentation is
weaker than the ESS's, but it fills the gap in cross-national EU-specific items — particularly
on trust in EU institutions and on perceived benefit from membership — at higher frequency
than the ESS.


# 7. Geographic identifiers in the datasets

Availability of geographic identifiers is the binding constraint on any analysis of regional
disparities, and it is the point on which the Polish and Hungarian cases differ most.

## 7.1. Polish administrative and statistical geography

```{=typst}
  columns: (auto, 1fr, 1fr, auto),
  stroke: none, inset: 5pt,
  table.hline(),
  table.header([*Level*], [*Polish name*], [*English name*], [*Count*]),

  [NUTS 1], [Makroregion], [Macroregion], [7],
  [NUTS 2], [Region], [Region (voivodeship; Mazowieckie split in two)], [17],
  [NUTS 3], [Podregion], [Subregion (groups of powiats)], [73],
  [LAU 1], [Powiat], [County (314 land + 66 city-counties)], [380],

  table.hline(),

```

```{=typst}
#align(center)[#text(size: 9pt, style: "italic")[Table 5. Polish administrative and statistical geography (as at 1 January 2025)]]
#v(0.6em)
```
Two points of detail matter. First, the **administrative** unit is the voivodeship
(*województwo*), of which there are 16; the **statistical** NUTS 2 level has 17 units because
Mazowieckie is divided into the Warsaw capital region and the surrounding Mazowiecki regional
unit. Surveys generally code the 16 administrative voivodeships, so mapping survey data onto
NUTS 2 statistics requires care for Mazowieckie in particular — and Mazowieckie is precisely
the unit where the Warsaw/periphery contrast is largest and most relevant to WP5. Second, the
present NUTS structure dates from the NUTS 2016 revision (effective 2018); the NUTS 2021 and
NUTS 2024 revisions introduced no changes for Poland, but earlier ESS rounds use the
pre-2018 coding.

Every unit carries a TERYT code issued by GUS, which is the join key for merging external
data — census results, GUS regional statistics, EU fund absorption figures and PKW election
results are all published on TERYT identifiers.

## 7.2. Geographic identifier availability


```{=typst}
#align(center)[#text(size: 9pt, style: "italic")[Table 6. Geographic identifier availability by dataset]]
#v(0.6em)
```
**CBOS APiW.** Voivodeship of residence is a sample-frame variable, present in every wave and
used both as a stratification variable and as a weighting margin. Settlement size class
(`KLM`) has six categories: village; town up to 19,999; 20,000–49,999; 50,000–99,999;
100,000–499,999; 500,000+. Later (CAPI-era) waves additionally carry a flag for whether the
locality is a city with powiat status, which is a coarse but genuine sub-voivodeship
distinction and separates the large urban centres from their hinterlands.

**ESS (Poland).** The `region` variable is coded at NUTS 2, with 16 units (PL11 Łódzkie, PL12
Mazowieckie, PL21 Małopolskie, PL22 Śląskie, PL31 Lubelskie, PL32 Podkarpackie, PL33
Świętokrzyskie, PL34 Podlaskie, PL41 Wielkopolskie, PL42 Zachodniopomorskie, PL43 Lubuskie,
PL51 Dolnośląskie, PL52 Opolskie, PL61 Kujawsko-Pomorskie, PL62 Warmińsko-Mazurskie, PL63
Pomorskie in the pre-2018 coding). `domicil` gives a five-category settlement type comparable
to the Hungarian variable.

## 7.3. Implications for research

- **Both** Polish datasets support voivodeship-level (NUTS 2) analysis in their standard
  public releases. This is a material advantage over the Hungarian case, where the TÁRKI
  Omnibusz offers only settlement type and NUTS 2/3 identification is confined to the ESS.
  The Polish and Hungarian analyses can be aligned at NUTS 2, but only the Polish one can be
  run at that level in both datasets.
- **Neither** dataset identifies powiat or gmina. Analyses requiring finer resolution —
  matching respondents to local EU fund absorption, to local labour market conditions or to
  commune-level election results — cannot be done with these releases. Three options exist:
  aggregate the contextual data to voivodeship and accept the loss of variance; commission a
  survey with settlement identifiers, as the Hungarian team has done with TÁRKI; or negotiate
  access to identified CBOS data.
- **Pooling is the practical route to regional precision.** A single CBOS wave of c. 1,000
  gives roughly 60 respondents per voivodeship, which will not support voivodeship estimates.
  But the waves are monthly and the core items are stable, so pooling waves within a year or
  a period yields usable voivodeship samples. This is the main methodological reason to prefer
  CBOS over the ESS for Task 5.2 on the Polish side, and it has no Hungarian counterpart
  because the Hungarian omnibus lacks the regional variable entirely.
- **The ESS regional caveat is binding.** As noted in Section 4.5, ESS documentation states
  that regional inference is not supported for Poland and recommends NUTS 1 grouping. Treat
  ESS regional breakdowns as descriptive.

The pattern to note is that the two datasets are strong in opposite places, and in a way that
is convenient. CBOS is stronger on **EU-specific substance** — membership support, benefit
assessment, the euro, EU funds — because those items were written for a national audience and
asked repeatedly. The ESS is stronger on **standardised psychometric and trust constructs** —
generalised trust, human values, political efficacy — because those are core ESS content. For
Task 5.3, which needs socioeconomic perception measured against EU attitudes, CBOS supplies
the EU side at high frequency and the ESS supplies the comparative and attitudinal-construct
side.

The distribution is informative in itself. Content peaks in 2002–2004 (accession negotiations,

salience and the limits of what has been deposited. Note that these counts are of questions
appearing in the *deposited* archive; the underlying monthly series is continuous.


# 10. Conclusion

This document has presented the Polish public opinion data landscape for the study of
post-enlargement socioeconomic disparities and euroscepticism:

1. **CBOS "Aktualne problemy i wydarzenia" (1990–present)**: a monthly national omnibus with
   329 waves (January 1990 – December 2017) deposited openly with full verbatim
   questionnaires, voivodeship-level geographic identification, and the longest continuous EU
   membership support series in the region.
2. **ESS Poland (2002–2024)**: eleven released rounds with cross-national comparability,
   NUTS 2 identification and documented methodological control.
3. **PGSW, POLPAN and Diagnoza Społeczna**: election behaviour, within-person change, and
   detailed household economic measurement respectively.

Key findings:

- Both principal datasets contain the core political, socioeconomic and EU attitude variables
  needed for Tasks 5.2 and 5.3.
- **Geographic identification is better in Poland than in Hungary.** Both Polish datasets
  carry a NUTS 2 identifier in their standard public releases, where the Hungarian omnibus
  carries only settlement type. Neither Polish dataset reaches powiat or gmina level, so
  fine-grained matching to local EU fund absorption or local election results is not possible
  without commissioned data or a negotiated release.
- **Pooling CBOS waves is the practical route to voivodeship-level estimates.** Monthly
  fieldwork with stable core items means that pooling within a year gives usable regional
  samples; no equivalent strategy is available on the Hungarian side.
- Appendix A catalogues 798 CBOS questions (630 tier A, 168 tier B) from 133
  waves between 1992 and 2017, classified by construct and reproduced verbatim in
  Polish. Of these, 27 distinct question texts recur in four or more waves and
  constitute the usable longitudinal series; these are listed separately in Appendix A.1.
- Appendix B catalogues the ESS Poland items with verbatim Polish wording and question
  numbers by round.
- **CBOS question coverage is uneven and politically driven.** Pre-2004 waves concentrate on
  accession and its expected costs and benefits; 2004–2014 on post-accession evaluation,
  labour mobility and the euro; 2015–2017 on refugees and migration. Researchers should not
  assume that absence of an item in a given year is random with respect to salience.
- **ESS coverage is more regular but narrower.** Trust in the European Parliament and in the
  United Nations appear in every round and give an unbroken 20-year series. The integration
  depth item (`euftf`) appears in every round except Round 5, where it was excluded from the
  source questionnaire. The EU membership referendum item (`vteurmmb`) is available only from
  Round 8 (2016). The most detailed immigration modules are Round 1 (2002) and Round 7 (2014).
- **The two sources answer different questions and should be used together.** The ESS
  establishes where Poland sits relative to other member states and supplies validated
  attitudinal constructs; CBOS establishes when Polish attitudes moved, and supports the
  regional disaggregation that Task 5.2 requires.

The most common constructs catalogued in Appendix A, by frequency, are:
EU / international orientation (other) (138), EU accession referendum: vote intention/turnout (101), Refugees (75), Support for EU membership / integration (74), NATO membership (65), European Parliament / EP elections (60), Assessment of costs/benefits of membership (52), Labour mobility / free movement of workers (38).

# Appendix A. Inventory of CBOS APiW Questions Related to European Integration

This appendix catalogues every question identified in the deposited CBOS "Aktualne problemy i
wydarzenia" documentation (1992–2017) that bears directly or indirectly on European
integration, EU attitudes, mobility, migration and international organisations. It was built
by parsing the verbatim questionnaires contained in the 165 deposited wave documentation
files whose metadata indicates EU-related content, and it reproduces the Polish wording as it
appears in those documents.

**Column key**

- **Wave** — APiW wave number with month and year of fieldwork (e.g. APiW 322 (III 2017)).
- **Q** — question identifier within that wave's questionnaire. Numeric identifiers are from
  the PAPI-era format; letter-prefixed identifiers (E1, M12A) are from the CADAS CAPI format.
- **Tier** — A = direct EU/European integration question; B = indirectly relevant (migration,
  NATO, international orientation).
- **Construct** — short English label for the measured concept, assigned by rule from the
  Polish wording.
- **Exact Polish wording** — verbatim question stem from the deposited questionnaire.

**A note on provenance and limits.** The Polish text is reproduced as extracted from the
archived PDFs. Extraction is faithful but mechanical: line breaks within a question stem are
joined, response categories are omitted from the table (they are in the source documents), and
very long stems are truncated with […]. Question numbering is not comparable across the
PAPI/CADAS format break described in Section 3.6. Construct labels are assigned by pattern
matching and should be treated as a navigation aid rather than as a validated coding. Before
using any item analytically, consult the wave's documentation PDF via the DOI given in
Appendix A.3.

# Appendix B. Inventory of ESS (Poland) Questions Related to European Integration

This appendix catalogues the ESS items bearing on European integration, international
institutional trust and immigration, with the verbatim Polish wording used in the Polish
fieldwork questionnaires and the question number for each round.

**Sources and limits.** The Polish wording is taken from the Polish translated questionnaires
archived by ESS for Rounds 3–11. **The Polish questionnaires for Rounds 1 and 2 are not in the
public ESS document archive**; for those rounds the question numbers below are taken from the
ESS source (English) questionnaire, and the Polish wording should be obtained from the ESS
Data Portal's national documentation or from the Polish national coordinator at IFiS PAN
before being quoted. Where an item's Polish wording is identical to the previous round, this
is stated rather than repeated.

**Column key.** Round/year; Q = question number in the Polish questionnaire; Variable = ESS
variable name; Construct; Exact Polish wording.


## B.1. Trust in the European Parliament and the United Nations

Both items sit inside the standard institutional trust battery, introduced by a common stem.
The battery stem in the Polish questionnaire reads:

```{=typst}
#block(inset: (left: 10pt), above: 0.6em, below: 0.8em)[
  #text(size: 9pt)[„KARTA 9 Posługując się tą kartą, proszę wskazać na skali od 0 do 10 na ile
  osobiście ma P. zaufanie do każdej z instytucji, którą wymienię. 0 oznacza całkowity brak
  zaufania wobec instytucji, a 10 oznacza, że ma P. do niej całkowite zaufanie. Pozostałe
  liczby służą do wyrażenia opinii pośrednich. Na ile ma P. zaufanie do… ODCZYTAĆ…"]
]
```

The two items of interest are `… Parlamentu Europejskiego?` (`trstep`) and `… Organizacji
Narodów Zjednoczonych?` (`trstun`), each answered on a 0–10 scale with 77 = refusal and 88 =
don't know. The showcard number and the battery position change between rounds; the item
wording does not.

```{=typst}
  [ESS11 (2023)], [B11], [B12], [0–10], [Polish questionnaire],
)
```

```{=typst}
#note[These are the most consistent longitudinal items in the Polish ESS series, present in
every round from 2002 to 2023 with identical wording and scale. Only the question number
changes. Together they give a two-decade series on international institutional trust; the gap
between them is interpretable as an EU-specific trust premium or deficit, and is directly
comparable with the Hungarian series.]
```

## B.4. Immigration: admission and perceived consequences

The six-item standard immigration battery is present in every round. The first three items
(`imsmetn`, `imdfetn`, `impcntr`) ask how far Poland should allow people to come and live
there — of the same ethnic group as the majority, of a different ethnic group, and from
poorer countries outside Europe respectively — on a four-point scale (Zezwalać dużej liczbie
osób / Zezwalać pewnej liczbie osób / Zezwalać tylko nielicznym / Nie zezwalać nikomu). The
second three (`imbgeco`, `imueclt`, `imwbcnt`) ask about perceived consequences on 0–10
scales.

```{=typst}
#block(inset: (left: 10pt), above: 0.6em, below: 0.4em)[
  #text(size: 9pt, weight: "bold")[imsmetn] #linebreak()
  #text(size: 9pt)[„Posługując się tą kartą, proszę powiedzieć, w jakim zakresie, P. zdaniem,
  państwo polskie powinno zezwalać ludziom należącym do tej samej rasy lub grupy etnicznej,
  co większość mieszkańców Polski, na przyjazd i zamieszkanie w Polsce? Czy Polska powinna:"]
  #v(0.45em)
  #text(size: 9pt, weight: "bold")[imdfetn] #linebreak()
  #text(size: 9pt)[„A jeśli chodzi o ludzi należących do innej rasy lub grupy etnicznej niż
  większość mieszkańców Polski? Proszę wybrać odpowiedź z tej samej karty."]
  #v(0.45em)
  #text(size: 9pt, weight: "bold")[impcntr] #linebreak()
  #text(size: 9pt)[„A jeśli chodzi o ludzi z biedniejszych krajów spoza Europy? Proszę wybrać
  odpowiedź z tej samej karty."]
  #v(0.45em)
  #text(size: 9pt, weight: "bold")[imbgeco] #linebreak()
  #text(size: 9pt)[„Czy P. zdaniem to, że ludzie z innych krajów przyjeżdżają, aby żyć
  w Polsce, jest ogólnie biorąc korzystne, czy też niekorzystne dla polskiej gospodarki?
  Odpowiadając, proszę posłużyć się tą kartą." (00 = Niekorzystne dla gospodarki, 10 =
  Korzystne dla gospodarki)]
  #v(0.45em)
  #text(size: 9pt, weight: "bold")[imueclt] #linebreak()
  #text(size: 9pt)[„Posługując się tą kartą, proszę powiedzieć, czy P. zdaniem to, że ludzie
  z innych krajów przyjeżdżają, aby żyć w Polsce, ogólnie biorąc, szkodzi życiu kulturalnemu
  w Polsce, czy też je wzbogaca?" (00 = Szkodzi życiu kulturalnemu, 10 = Wzbogaca życie
  kulturalne)]
  #v(0.45em)
  #text(size: 9pt, weight: "bold")[imwbcnt] #linebreak()
  #text(size: 9pt)[„Czy w wyniku tego, że ludzie z innych krajów przyjeżdżają do Polski
  i żyją tutaj, Polska stała się gorszym czy lepszym miejscem do życia? Odpowiadając, proszę
  posłużyć się tą kartą." (00 = Gorszym miejscem do życia, 10 = Lepszym miejscem do życia)]
]
```

```{=typst}
including items on the perceived origin, skills and economic contribution of migrants — which
are the appropriate source for any fine-grained analysis of immigration attitudes. For Poland,
ESS7 is the last measurement before the 2015 refugee crisis and is therefore the natural
baseline against which the CBOS 2015–2017 series (Appendix A) should be read.]
```

## B.5. EU-wide redistribution and EU-level decision-making (ESS8 only)

Round 8 (2016) carried two items in the welfare module that bear directly on preferences over
the level at which social policy should be decided.

```{=typst}
#block(inset: (left: 10pt), above: 0.6em, below: 0.4em)[
  #text(size: 9pt, weight: "bold")[E37 — EU-wide social benefit scheme] #linebreak()
  #text(size: 9pt)[„Proponuje się, aby wprowadzić program świadczeń społecznych dla wszystkich
  osób ubogich na terenie całej Unii Europejskiej. […] Czy, ogólnie rzecz biorąc, byłby/-aby
  P. za czy przeciwko wprowadzeniu takiego programu świadczeń społecznych na terenie całej
  Unii Europejskiej?" (1 = Zdecydowanie przeciw … 4 = Zdecydowanie za)]
  #v(0.5em)
  #text(size: 9pt, weight: "bold")[E38 — effect of shifting decisions to EU level] #linebreak()
  #text(size: 9pt)[„Gdyby więcej decyzji zapadało na poziomie Unii Europejskiej, a nie na
  poziomie rządów poszczególnych krajów, to czy uważa P., że świadczenia społeczne i usługi
  socjalne w Polsce poprawiłyby się czy pogorszyły?" (1 = Znacznie poprawiłyby się … 5 =
  Znacznie by się pogorszyły)]
]
```

```{=typst}
#note[The showcard for E37 sets out three design features of the hypothetical scheme,
including that richer member states would contribute more than poorer ones. Because Poland is
a net recipient, responses to this item are not directly comparable with those from net
contributor states without accounting for that asymmetry — a point that applies equally to the
Hungarian data and should be handled consistently across the two national analyses.]
```

## B.6. Allocation of authority (ESS1 only)

Round 1 (2002) carried an item asking respondents to allocate decision-making authority over
a set of policy areas between the international, European, national and regional levels. It
is the only ESS measurement of multi-level authority preferences, has no later counterpart,
and was fielded in Poland in the year before the accession referendum. The Polish wording is
not in the public ESS document archive and should be obtained from the Polish national
documentation.
